clue.text: Draw out with small lure

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
to educe is to draw out or bring forth something latent

explanation.surface: A fisherman coaxes a catch to the surface with a modest bait.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw out' and 'lure' both look like fishing talk, but 'Draw out' is the wordplay and 'lure' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To seduce is to tempt or entice someone astray, which is what a lure does.

clue.text: Film director Nick capturing singular area of London

indicators.note: capturing means the word for nick holds the next letter within it

parts.note: to nick is to score, i.e. cut a notch
S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular
SE is the south-east postal district of London

explanation.surface: A film director named Nick is shooting in a single district of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a first name; it is a verb meaning to cut a notch.
explanation.definitionFit: Martin Scorsese is the American director of Taxi Driver and Goodfellas.

clue.text: Challenging to maintain Noel's oddly neglected leaf remover

indicators.note: to maintain is to hold, so the first word keeps the other letters inside it

parts.note: challenging authority is being defiant

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters are neglected, leaving the even ones

explanation.surface: A defiant Noel's garden chemical, its odd details overlooked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly neglected' drops the odd letters of the name and its apostrophe-S, keeping only the even ones.
explanation.definitionFit: A defoliant is a chemical sprayed to strip foliage from plants.

clue.text: Burn Map? Not entirely

indicators.note: not entirely means the word is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: a chart is a map, especially a nautical one

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether to burn the map and gets a half-hearted answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To char is to scorch or blacken by burning.

clue.text: Children's items of personal laundry almost burn

indicators.note: almost means the last letter of the laundry word is dropped

parts.note: smalls is British slang for underwear in the wash
to fry is to burn or cook in hot fat, or to burn in the sun

explanation.surface: Children's underwear has almost been scorched in the wash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Children's' reads as 'Children is': SMALLS is British slang for underwear, cut to SMALL.
explanation.definitionFit: Small fry is an idiom for young children or unimportant people, like tiny fish.

clue.text: "Little time left" — something said after a month

indicators.note: after places the trimmed saying behind the month abbreviation

parts.note: MO is an abbreviation of month

indicators.note: left means the time letter departs from the saying

parts.note: a dictum is a saying or pronouncement

explanation.surface: A quotation warns that little time is left, voiced a month later.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little time left' looks like the opening quote; only 'Little' is the definition, and 'time left' deletes T.
explanation.definitionFit: A modicum is a small amount, so 'little' in the sense of a bit.

clue.text: Dull school subject fewer longing to pursue? Just the opposite

indicators.note: the clue says longing follows, then reverses that, so it comes first

parts.note: lust is strong longing or desire
RE is religious education, a British school subject
less, loosely, means fewer

explanation.surface: A dull school subject attracts fewer pupils keen to take it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to pursue' would put longing last; 'Just the opposite' puts it first. Religious education is a standard British school subject.
explanation.definitionFit: Lustreless means lacking sheen or gloss, hence dull in appearance.

clue.text: Passage covering king's accidental success

indicators.note: covering means the passage word goes over and around the king's letter

parts.note: a flue is a passage for smoke in a chimney
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A secret passage hiding the king turns out a lucky break.
explanation.definitionFit: A fluke is a lucky chance, a success won by accident rather than skill.

clue.text: Unsettled by you once when extremely touchy

parts.note: ye is an archaic form of you
as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

indicators.note: extremely means only the extreme letters of the word are used

explanation.surface: Someone is rattled by an old acquaintance when feeling particularly sensitive.
explanation.definitionFit: Yeasty means frothy and in ferment, hence restless or unsettled.

clue.text: Peto, overwhelmed by unbridled greed, becomes more irritable

indicators.note: overwhelmed by means the setter's letter is swallowed inside the other letters
unbridled means unrestrained, so the letters run wild into a new order

parts.note: Peto is the setter, who refers to themselves as I

explanation.surface: The setter, swamped by rampant greed, grows tetchier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unbridled' rearranges GREED to EDGER, with I inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Edgy means tense and on edge, so edgier is nervier or more irritable.

clue.text: Offensively nonchalant worker introduced to sour newspaper boss

indicators.note: introduced to means the worker is placed inside the other letters

parts.note: milk that is off has gone sour
ED is short for editor
a hand is a manual worker, as in farmhand

explanation.surface: A new staffer meets a grumpy editor who treats them coolly.
explanation.definitionFit: Offhanded describes a casual, curt manner that can seem rude or dismissive.

clue.text: We object likewise before facing Arsenal's top scorer

parts.note: so means likewise, as in 'so do I'
us is the object form of the pronoun we

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Fans object before facing Arsenal's leading goal-getter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scorer' suggests football goals but means a composer who writes scores.
explanation.definitionFit: John Philip Sousa was an American composer of marches, so one who writes musical scores.

clue.text: Only part of the foot

definitions.meaning: ... means only, as in the ... survivor

explanation.definitionFit: Sole means single or only, and is also the underside of the foot.

clue.text: Cut by most recent hazard for swimmers

parts.note: to rip is to tear or cut
current means latest or most recent

explanation.surface: Swimmers are warned of the latest danger after someone gets a cut.
explanation.definitionFit: A rip current is a strong seaward flow that can drag swimmers out.

clue.text: Spoke with Matt about accepting roubles in cash trading facility

indicators.note: accepting means the shuffled letters take in the currency letter
about signals the letters being moved around

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for the rouble, Russia's currency

explanation.surface: Someone discussed taking Russian currency at a cash exchange with Matt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges the two names' letters to SPOTMAKET, and 'accepting' takes the rouble letter inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A spot market is one where goods or currencies trade for cash and immediate delivery.

clue.text: Republican severely criticises left- leaning photographer

indicators.note: leaning to the left means the letters are read right to left

parts.note: to pan is to criticise harshly

explanation.surface: A Republican attacks a photographer with leftist sympathies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left-leaning' looks political but reverses REP PANS.
explanation.definitionFit: Snapper is informal for a photographer, one who takes snaps.

clue.text: Strangely mute about 50s hairstyle

indicators.note: about means the shuffled letters go around the other pair
strangely signals the letters in an unusual order

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty, so two fifties are LL

explanation.surface: A curiously silent man sports a 1950s haircut.
explanation.walkthrough: '50s' looks like a decade; it is two Roman fifties. 'Strangely' gives MUET, and 'about' wraps it round them.
explanation.definitionFit: The mullet is a haircut short at the front and long at the back.

clue.text: Cleric fails in objective when surrounded

indicators.note: in places the shuffled letters inside the objective word

parts.note: an end is an aim or objective

indicators.note: fails suggests the word breaking down into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A clergyman falls short of his goal when hemmed in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fails' rearranges the clergyman's letters into a ring shape, which 'in' sets inside the goal word.
explanation.definitionFit: Encircled means ringed round on all sides.

clue.text: Make mistakes as a swimmer

explanation.definitionFit: Flounder means to struggle or blunder, and is also a flatfish.

clue.text: Sets forth with volunteers in groups heading west

indicators.note: in an across answer heading west means reading right to left
in places the volunteers inside the groups

parts.note: sets are groups
TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve

explanation.surface: Volunteers set off westward in small parties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' gives SETATS, which 'heading west' turns round. The TA (Territorial Army) is the British Army's volunteer reserve.
explanation.definitionFit: To state is to set forth or declare formally.

clue.text: Starts to play expertly right after miss by captain

indicators.note: after puts the remaining letters behind the word for miss

parts.note: to skip is to miss out

indicators.note: starts of words are their first letters

explanation.surface: A captain begins to play skilfully after sitting a game out.
explanation.definitionFit: A skipper is the captain of a team or a ship.

clue.text: Tommy for instance makes ridiculous claim about you and me

indicators.note: about means the shuffled letters go round the pronoun
ridiculous suggests the letters are absurdly jumbled

parts.note: you and me together are us

explanation.surface: Someone named Tommy makes an absurd claim about the two of us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tommy' looks like a person; it is The Who's rock opera. 'ridiculous' gives MICAL, which 'about' wraps round the pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: Tommy, the rock opera by The Who, was staged as a musical show.

clue.text: Complained when half-hearted girl's employed in government department

indicators.note: employed in places the girl inside the department

parts.note: MOD is the UK Ministry of Defence

indicators.note: half-hearted means half of the middle letters is lost

parts.note: Anne is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A lacklustre girl working in a ministry grumbled.
explanation.walkthrough: ANNE loses one of its two central Ns, leaving ANE. The MOD is Britain's Ministry of Defence.
explanation.definitionFit: To moan is to grumble, so moaned means complained.

clue.text: Port contributing to slipshod essay

indicators.note: contributing to says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A port gets a mention in a sloppy piece of student writing.
explanation.definitionFit: Odessa is a major Black Sea port city in Ukraine.

clue.text: I talk with Pat largely about the German's earlier book

indicators.note: earlier puts the German article in front of the rest

parts.note: das is the German for the (neuter)

indicators.note: about signals the letters being moved around
largely means most of the name, so its last letter goes

explanation.surface: Someone discusses an early work by a German thinker with Pat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'largely' cuts PAT to PA; 'about' rearranges ITALK PA to KAPITAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Das Kapital is Karl Marx's major work on political economy.

clue.text: Piece of sporting equipment for society girl

parts.note: Kate is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A debutante's sports kit is the subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'society girl' reads as a debutante but splits into S and KATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A skate is a boot with a blade or wheels used in skating sports.

clue.text: German-speaking woman's deceit ultimately ignored

indicators.note: ultimately points at the final letter, which is ignored

parts.note: fraud is deceit or trickery

explanation.surface: A German woman's lies are finally overlooked.
explanation.definitionFit: Frau is German for a married woman or wife, used as a title like Mrs.

clue.text: Complain about priest turning up

parts.note: CA is circa, Latin for about

indicators.note: in a down answer turning up means read from the bottom upwards

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles about a clergyman who turns up.
explanation.definitionFit: To carp is to find fault or grumble pettily.

clue.text: Essential to punish Arkansas swindler

indicators.note: Essential to says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Arkansas must punish a conman.
explanation.definitionFit: A shark is slang for a predatory cheat or con artist, as in loan shark.

clue.text: Won through being positive before vicar felt unwell

indicators.note: before puts the positive letter in front

parts.note: Rev is short for Reverend, a vicar's title
ailed means was sick

explanation.surface: Optimism triumphed until the vicar was taken ill.
explanation.definitionFit: To prevail is to triumph after a struggle, which is to win through.

clue.text: Crack Australian forward not starting very well

parts.note: pert means cheeky or forward

indicators.note: not starting means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: sure means very well, as in 'sure, I'll come'

explanation.surface: A cheeky Aussie forward lacks the strong start that would make him a top player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack' looks like an adjective for a top player; it means a gap.
explanation.definitionFit: An aperture is an opening or gap, such as a crack.

clue.text: Spinner needing rest

definitions.meaning: in snooker a ... is a raised rest for the cue

explanation.walkthrough: In snooker, a cue-sport, the spider is a raised rest for the cue.
explanation.definitionFit: A spider spins silk, and the snooker spider is a cue rest.
